chunks: "Process is the unit-to-unit spread: the IC's reference might be ±1% or so, the oscillator ±10%, the current limit ±20%, FET resistance varies, and the inductor and capacitors have their own tolerances, say ±20% on L and a lot more on a derated ceramic.
Voltage is the input range, the output and the load.
A wide input changes the duty cycle: at maximum input the duty is smallest, ripple current is largest, switching loss is highest and the on-time is shortest, which can hit the minimum on-time.
Temperature raises resistance: copper DCR goes up 0. 39% per °C and FET R DS(on) rises about half a percent per °C, so efficiency drops when hot, and that heats the part further.
Hot ferrite inductors saturate at lower current, ceramics change capacitance, cold electrolytics have much higher ESR.
For the output accuracy the stack-up is reference, divider tolerance and regulation, giving around ±2. 5% in my 1% example.
For the loop, the worst case is usually low effective capacitance at light load, and for thermal it's maximum input, full load, hot.

I'd verify at corners on the bench and design margins: current limit above the load including tolerance, saturation above the maximum limit hot, ripple within spec at maximum input with the oscillator and inductor at their tolerance extremes."
